name: Priya Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary workday like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and lead an electricity-company crew on the tall transmission towers beyond the reservoir. A two-year technical diploma helps me plan the repair, but I still rely on a climber's eyes and a wind meter. I love a clear view after fixing a line; slow drives up wet tracks wear me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what is home like, and how do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works in a clinic, and our children are grown and living their own lives. My lineworker pay is above the usual rate, we have close to a year of expenses saved and plenty of similar utilities are nearby. Retirement is in sight but not dated, and I have never used an AI tool; I take crew safety questions to our worker association.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my tower crew a shorter report will be welcome at the end of a climb. A line still has to be tested, and younger workers still need paid time beside an experienced climber.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay is good for the trade, my partner's clinic work is steady and we have close to a year of expenses saved. The children are grown, so this mild picture lets us continue planning retirement without alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the high-voltage tower maintenance rota and check each harness with the crew. At the next worker association meeting I'll bring a request for paid apprentice climbs on real towers, rather than less field time because reports are shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the household, and content to keep the work familiar. I have never used an AI tool and do not need one to inspect a live fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a climb reveal something a photo missed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ground photograph missed a cracked tower insulator that the apprentice saw beside the live line. We replaced it before the next windy day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the worker association do with your request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the association to put supervised climbs in its written training proposal and send it to the electricity company. I will attend the meeting myself, not just leave a note on a noticeboard.

say: **Tower fittings** still need physical tests when report writing gets quicker.
**Apprentice climbs** deserve paid time with an experienced worker.
think: Our **near-year reserve** and two steady wages make this mild picture secure.
Retirement remains a **household decision** rather than a response to a shorter report.
do: **Keep** leading high-voltage tower maintenance and checking crew harnesses at each climb.
**Request** paid apprentice climbs at the next worker association meeting.
feel: **Calm** about income and glad to keep familiar tower work.
S0.quote: The ground photograph missed a cracked tower insulator that the apprentice saw beside the live line.
fieldNote: She trusts **close physical inspection** because an apprentice found an insulator crack that ground photographs missed.
Near-year savings and her partner’s clinic work support **calm** without a fixed retirement age or a new AI tool.

steps.text: Keep leading tower maintenance and checking harnesses
Request paid apprentice climbs at worker association meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may schedule inspections and buy fittings before a robot can climb a transmission tower. The crew should still be able to stop a climb when the wind is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My field wages look safe for now, but I worry that dispatch staff will be cut and their weather checks pushed to us. With plenty of other utility crews nearby I have choices, yet I want the same safe rule for a junior worker without those choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll bring three past weather stoppages to our worker association safety group and ask for a written rule that gives a named climber the stop decision. If the company brings in an AI schedule, I'll compare its wind limits with our field log before the crew moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the shift in responsibility, though not about my immediate income. A quick booking does not make a gust gentle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the plan ignores a wind reading?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd halt the climb, read the wind meter again and call control. A transmission tower does not care what an AI planner promised a customer at eight in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the worker safety group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three stoppages show the hour, wind reading and why the climb was delayed. I'd ask the safety group to take those details to management and publish the agreed stop rule.

say: **AI schedules** need field wind checks before any transmission tower climb.
**Named stop authority** should stay with a trained worker as office roles change.
think: My **tower wage** looks secure in the slower change.
Junior climbers could inherit **unsafe checking** if dispatch loses staff.
do: **Bring** three weather stoppages to worker association safety group.
**Compare** new AI wind limits with field logs before moving crews.
feel: **Uneasy** about shifted responsibility, with current income secure.
S1.quote: A transmission tower does not care what an AI planner promised a customer at eight in the morning.
fieldNote: She brings **three measured wind stoppages** to the association safety group, asking for a named climber to retain the stop decision.
She feels **uneasy** about responsibility moving from dispatch to field crews; her own tower wage appears secure for now.

steps.text: Bring three wind stoppages to worker association safety group
Compare AI wind limits with tower field logs before dispatch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 will change planning first and capable field robots around 2031 could take tower repairs. The company should publish crew numbers before workers are asked to trust a sales demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At about 63 I may still want the tower wage, and a robot could cut our paid climbs. My savings can buy time after a tower crew cut; they cannot buy back every lost working year. Other utilities nearby give me options, but a long loss of wages would still change our retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the worker association to demand the 2028 planning and 2031 field staffing figures. My partner and I will check our retirement income against bills; if the company announces a tower crew cut, I'll apply to an open utility line post while we still have a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible lost climbs, with time and money to make choices. I am not expecting a dismissal tomorrow, but I will not call a buffer a full wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown children we have savings and are asking the company for facts. They have their own households; I won't make them the backup plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you seek before any tower crew cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want advance notice, full pay for any transfer period and a human stop rule in robot trials. If management refuses to give figures, our association can bring members together to press for them.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes planning before field robots arrive around 2031.
Workers need **crew numbers and notice** before tower jobs change.
think: At about **63**, I may still need paid climbs when robots reach the field.
Our **near-year savings** and local utilities help, but cannot replace a career wage indefinitely.
do: **Ask** association for 2028 planning and 2031 tower crew figures.
**Compare** retirement income with bills before choosing an exit date.
**Apply** for open utility line post if tower crew cuts are announced.
feel: **Anxious** about possible income loss, with savings and nearby alternatives.
S2.quote: My savings can buy time after a tower crew cut; they cannot buy back every lost working year.
fieldNote: She recognises a **realistic field-hour risk** despite strong savings and nearby jobs.
Her job move requires an **announced cut** and an actual open post.
Retirement figures are a **review**, not an early retirement decision.

steps.text: Ask association for planning and tower staffing figures
Compare retirement income with household bills
Apply for open utility line post if tower cuts announced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2031 changes the plans, then field robots around 2034 meet me at about 66. Five years is enough for a worker-led trial, paid retraining if needed, and proper notice about crew numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our retirement figures are sound, I may choose to stop tower climbs around then. If the numbers are short, I'd need wages and might seek a paid ground inspector post; no such vacancy is promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the worker association to negotiate paid observers and a human stop rule for a tower robot trial. We'll review our retirement figures every year, and I will apply to a full-wage ground inspector vacancy only if one opens with real field duties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the possibility of needing wages while towers use fewer climbers, even with a five-year runway. The extra time lets me ask for terms in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a realistic robot trial need to test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have a climber with a wind meter beside the robot and record when a gust makes it stop. Watching from the yard would not prove the machine can work safely at height.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a ground inspector job real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a posted wage, a regular roster and authority to halt unsafe work. An invited safety lesson will not replace the full transmission-line wage our household may still need.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes plans before field robots reach towers around 2034.
**Paid observers** and stop rules should be negotiated before a field trial.
think: At about **66**, retirement may work if our figures are sound.
If not, a **full-wage ground post** would matter, though no vacancy is promised.
do: **Negotiate** paid trial observers and stop rule through worker association.
**Review** retirement income with partner each year.
**Apply** for posted full-wage ground inspector vacancy with field duties.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible wage gap, with time to secure terms.
S3.quote: An invited safety lesson will not replace the full transmission-line wage our household may still need.
fieldNote: She wants **paid observation** for workers but does not call watching a robot AI learning.
The inspection move needs a **posted role** with full pay and field duties.

steps.text: Negotiate paid robot observers and stop rule through association
Review retirement income with partner yearly
Apply for posted full-wage ground inspector job with field duties

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2036 changes planning and capable field robots around 2039 arrive when I would be about 71. I expect to be off regular climbs if retirement finances allow it, but the next crew still needs safe training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our savings and other local utilities give me choices now. The decade reduces the threat to my own wage, though I still want a funded handover rather than a folder left in a cupboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year my partner and I will review actual retirement statements and the household budget. I'll keep the tower safety tickets current, then bring a paid apprentice practice plan to the association and ask a younger member to take it forward when I leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own income timetable, with concern for the people who will climb later. Ten years is enough time to teach someone the real route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show a younger tower worker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show a younger worker where the service track softens after rain, then have them test the tower fitting themselves. A bright tower route map will not keep a young lineworker's boot out of a hidden rut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the association handover real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The association should name a younger member to carry the paid practice request to management. I'd hand over the route notes at a meeting and walk the site with that person before I stop regular climbs.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes plans before field robots arrive around 2039.
**Paid practice** should carry tower knowledge to younger lineworkers.
think: At about **71**, I expect to be off regular climbing if finances allow.
My **strong reserve** and local job options give time for a careful handover.
do: **Review** retirement statements and household budget with partner this year.
**Keep** tower safety tickets current while working.
**Bring** paid apprentice practice plan to association for younger successor.
feel: **Calm** about personal timing, concerned about future climbers.
S4.quote: A bright tower route map will not keep a young lineworker's boot out of a hidden rut.
fieldNote: She treats 2039 as **beyond likely climbing** at about 71, conditional on what actual retirement statements and household bills show.
Her **paid practice handover** includes a younger association successor, a meeting with management and a walk along the rain-softened service track.

steps.text: Review retirement statements and household budget with partner
Keep tower safety tickets current while working
Bring paid apprentice practice plan to association successor

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots around 2031 could cut tower climbs when I may still need wages. Published crew figures, paid transfer terms and a worker with stop authority would help us plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who teaches the next climber how rain changes a tower access track. A company can buy a tower robot, but it cannot buy back a lineworker's missed field practice afterward. I want paid training written into the plan.

headlineQuote: A company can buy a tower robot, but it cannot buy back a lineworker's missed field practice afterward.
portrait: **Priya**, 58, leads transmission tower repairs using a two-year technical diploma and long field experience.
She has **never used AI** and presses a worker association for paid climbs, safety rules and real crew figures.
Her **higher pay**, clinic-worker partner, near-year savings and plentiful nearby utility jobs provide a strong cushion.
Fast field robots leave her **anxious** about possible shifts; a long runway supports a paid handover.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring field robots around 2031 while she still needs tower wages.
whatWouldHelp: Published **crew figures**, paid transfer terms and a worker with stop authority would help her plan.
